title: RFC: separate secret injection from destination-bound secret use
body:
Thanks for putting this together — the existing invariants are unusually strong for such a new tool: refs-only discovery, fixed failure messages around plaintext, no automatic write retries, read-back verification, and explicit service-account narrowing.

I think there is one security boundary worth naming early because it affects the core promise.

## Problem

Today `2password run` keeps a value out of the model/context while resolving it, but then places it in an agent-chosen child process environment and streams that child's stdout/stderr back normally.

That is useful **secret injection**, but it is not yet enforceable **secret use without reveal**: a compromised/prompt-injected agent can choose a child that prints the variable or sends it to an arbitrary destination.

I would keep `run` — it is useful — but distinguish it from a stronger capability.

## Proposed model

Keep 1Password as **custody** and make 2password the narrow **authority + private execution** layer:

```
1Password custody
    ↓ op:// handle
2password authority
    ↓ short-lived capability
private executor
    ↓
destination
    ↓
sanitized receipt
```

The key split is:

- `secret.use`: the caller may cause an allowed operation with a secret but never receive the value.
- `secret.reveal`: the caller may receive plaintext. `read` / `env resolve` are explicitly in this class.
- `run` remains an injection primitive and should document that the child is inside the trust boundary.

## Smallest strong primitive

A structured destination-bound request path, e.g. `2password request` / `2password broker http`:

- secret identified only by `op://...`
- exact HTTPS destination host
- no redirects, userinfo, or caller-controlled host override
- resolve/check public IPs before connect
- secret inserted internally into an approved header/field
- bounded response size
- redact exact injected values if the destination echoes them
- return a typed receipt, never the credential

This is much easier to reason about than trying to make arbitrary `run` commands non-revealing.

## Authority / leases

For unattended agents, machine identity should authenticate the caller but initially grant zero resources.

A human approval can mint a short-lived lease bound to:

`principal + resource + field + capability + destination + resource version/fingerprint + expiry + atomic use budget`

That gives us "approve once for this exact use" without turning a service-account token into blanket vault authority. Rotation invalidates stale leases automatically via the resource fingerprint/version.

## PII / egress

Two layers, deliberately separate:

1. **Destination binding/private execution is the privacy boundary.**
2. PII/secret redaction on tool/provider egress is a last guardrail for accidental echo, not an authorization mechanism.

Receipts should contain only bounded metadata: action, handle/item identity, destination, outcome, timing, and lease/use counters.

## Service-account note

The existing dedicated-vault service account is a good narrowing mechanism. Longer-term I would avoid treating "token is in Keychain" as authority by itself: an arbitrary local agent running as the same user should not inherit the ability to turn that token into unrestricted plaintext reads. Ideally the broker is the only component that can exercise it.

## Incremental path

1. Document the current `run` / `env run` trust boundary.
2. Add the structured destination-bound request primitive with exact-secret echo redaction and tests.
3. Add policy + non-secret receipts.
4. Add caller identity and short-lived leases for unattended use.
5. Only then consider a resident broker/daemon if prompt reduction justifies it.

## Non-goals

- replacing 1Password as custody
- weakening the existing "writes run once" invariant
- generic authenticated HTTP as a giant new surface
- using PII detection as the primary security boundary
- trying to make arbitrary child-process execution provably model-blind

## Provenance / related work

This builds directly on the security shape already established here by @kitlangton.

Related experiments/design work that may save us from re-learning the same edges:

- NousResearch/hermes-agent#107700 — destination-bound credential handles / `use != reveal`
- NousResearch/hermes-agent#107698 — why process-wide env hydration is the wrong long-term boundary
- NousResearch/hermes-agent#102922 — local PII egress redaction, explicitly treated as a guardrail rather than the privacy boundary
- pass-cli/passd experiments: zero-authority machine identities, exact HITL leases, destination binding, and sanitized receipts

Happy to implement the smallest slice rather than trying to land the whole architecture at once.

title: docs: clarify child-process secret boundary
body:
Small first slice from #1.

This does not change behavior. It makes the current trust boundary explicit in the README, security policy, and shipped agent skill:

- `read` / `env resolve` are explicit reveal/materialization paths.
- `run` / `env run` keep values out of 2password's own output, argv, and template files, but intentionally place plaintext in the selected child environment.
- The child therefore has to be trusted with the credential; arbitrary child execution is not a non-reveal security boundary.

I kept this deliberately small so the stronger destination-bound `secret.use` work can be discussed separately in #1.

Credit: this is documenting the boundary already implied by @kitlangton's existing `Op.exec`, explicit reveal commands, and no-leak invariants rather than changing those semantics.

Tests: docs/skill only; no runtime changes.

title: docs: clarify the secret execution boundary
body:
## Summary

Clarifies the existing security boundary without changing behavior:

- distinguishes intentional plaintext escape hatches (`read`, `env resolve`) from `run` / `env run`
- notes that the target child process receives plaintext and 1Password output masking is best effort
- makes the same rule explicit in the shipped agent skill
- documents that 2password is a credential-use surface, not an OS sandbox

This seems especially important for coding agents because a reference-only interface can otherwise look stronger than the underlying process boundary actually is.

## Why now

1Password's current CLI beta release notes explicitly clarify that `op run` stdout/stderr masking is best effort and does not guarantee concealment:
https://releases.1password.com/developers/cli-beta/2.40.0/

No runtime behavior changes here.

## Credit / provenance

Kit: the existing invariants in `AGENTS.md` already establish the strong foundations here—no secret argv, fixed errors around reveal paths, verified writes, no write retries, and fail-closed saved-account behavior. This PR only makes the remaining child-process boundary explicit in the user-facing docs and skill.

1Password: credit for explicitly documenting the best-effort nature of `op run` masking in the September 24, 2026 CLI beta notes.

title: feat: support Windows
body:
On Windows, the read-only commands and desktop-authenticated `run` already worked. Writes, `--clipboard`, `--stdin`, the saved service account, and the token stripping in `run`/`env run` did not, because they rely on macOS or POSIX tools (`pbpaste`, `cat`, `sh`, `env -u`, `osascript`). This PR adds a Windows path for each one. The macOS code paths and the security invariants in AGENTS.md stay the same.

## Runtime

- **Private input.** `--clipboard` reads through `powershell Get-Clipboard -Raw`, with stdout as the only channel. `--stdin` is read in-process with `Bun.stdin`, because there is no `cat`. Values still never touch argv.
- **Plaintext to op.** Bun's spawner already gives `op.exe` a real pipe on Windows, so the `sh -c 'cat | exec op "$@"'` wrapper is skipped there and the input goes straight to op's stdin. Every other part of `Op.op`, including the fixed `failure` messages, is shared.
- **Saved service account.** `src/credential.win.ps1` implements the same four operations as `keychain.jxa.js` (`get`, `exists`, `add`, `remove`). It stores the token DPAPI-encrypted (CurrentUser scope, with the service/account pair as entropy) in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.kitlangton.2password\`. The token crosses stdin and stdout only. `add` refuses to overwrite, and `remove` deletes the folder once it is empty. I chose DPAPI over Credential Manager because Credential Manager blobs are capped at 2,560 bytes and tokens can be longer. The opt-in store test uses about 9 KB. `status` and `setup` now report `storage: "windows-dpapi"` instead of a hard-coded `macos-keychain`.
- **Token stripping.** In place of `env -u OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`, op runs `src/without-token.ts`, which deletes the variable and then spawns the command with the terminal attached. It passes the exit code through and handles `.cmd` commands such as `npx`.
- **Settings path.** It falls back to `USERPROFILE` when `HOME` is unset, which is the normal case in PowerShell and cmd.

Security difference: macOS Keychain items carry an ACL. A DPAPI file can be decrypted by any process running as the same Windows user. On Windows, the narrow automation vault is therefore the real boundary. SKILL.md now says so.

## Tests and repo hygiene

- Windows can't execute the `#!/bin/sh` fakes, and Node refuses some arguments for `.cmd` files. `test/shim.ts` is compiled once per Bun version, then hard-linked into each sandbox as `op.exe` and the other fakes. Each link forwards to Git's `sh` with the original script. PATH still holds only the sandbox, plus Git's `usr/bin` for `sh`, `cat` and `printf`. I confirmed that the real `op` and `powershell` cannot be resolved from that PATH.
- Fixtures map `powershell` calls back onto `pbpaste`/`osascript` (`test/fixtures/platform.ts`), so recorded calls and assertions are identical on both platforms. The service-account and clipboard suites now run on Windows too. The one platform-specific assertion is the `run` argv (`env -u` vs. the helper). `bun run test:keychain` covers the DPAPI store on Windows.
- `.gitattributes` forces LF. With Git for Windows' default `core.autocrlf=true`, checkouts had CRLF and `oxfmt --check` failed on every file.
- `CLAUDE.md` is a symlink, which Windows checks out as a text file containing `AGENTS.md`. It is now in oxfmt's `ignorePatterns`, so formatting can't turn it into a regular file.

## Verification

On Windows 11 (build 26200), `bun run check` and `bun run test:keychain` pass. Against a real 1Password account, I ran these by hand:
- `service-account setup --create-vault --write --save-vault Personal`, with `verified: true`;
- `status`;
- `create api-credential` with `--stdin` and with `--clipboard`;
- `find`;
- `env run` and `run --env`.

All of them ran without desktop prompts after setup. The child process received the secret and did not see `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`.

Not verified: I have not run the suite on macOS after this change. The macOS branches are unchanged apart from the `Auth.storage` constant and the shared refactor in `keychain()`, but CI is the first macOS run. I did not add a Windows CI job.

title: feat: add destination-bound private requests
body:
Builds on #1 and the merged trust-boundary docs in #2.

This is intentionally only the next small slice: a structured private executor for simple authenticated HTTPS GETs. No leases/policy/daemon in this PR.

### Boundary

`2password request`:

- accepts the credential only as an `op://` reference
- supports only HTTPS port 443
- supports only `Authorization` or `X-API-Key`
- validates the complete URL before reading the credential
- resolves **all** destination addresses first and rejects the destination if any answer is private/reserved/special-use
- pins the TLS connection to one validated address, so there is no second DNS lookup
- never follows redirects
- limits the response to 64 KiB and 15 seconds
- keeps the entire response body private
- returns only bounded receipt metadata: status, bytes, safe destination path, exact-destination fingerprint, and exact-secret echo count

The response body staying private is deliberate: exact-secret redaction would still allow unrelated PII or a newly minted token to escape back to the agent.

### Tests

Tests cover:

- mixed public/private DNS answers fail **before** the credential resolver runs
- unsafe URL/header shapes fail before DNS or secret resolution
- special-use IPv4/IPv6 ranges
- terminal-newline normalization
- exact/JSON-escaped secret echo accounting
- response PII never enters the receipt
- CLI help path without touching `op` or the network

This is rebased on current main, including #5's Windows support, so the repository's macOS + Windows CI matrix can exercise it.

Follow-up, separately: short-lived use leases / caller authority. Keeping that out here so the private-execution primitive can be reviewed on its own.

### Verification

Current head `5240dfc08e1d3a1edbb8141542e4d98f4b93e0d5` / follow-up Effect v4 fixes passed the repository's full CI matrix:

- macOS: `bun run check` + package hygiene ✅
- Windows: `bun run check` + package hygiene + real DPAPI `test:keychain` ✅

The branch is based on upstream `0.2.0` and preserves the new `doctor`, `find`, Windows, and purpose changes.

title: fix: make service-account wording cross-platform
body:
Windows support shipped in 0.2.0, but a few shared service-account paths still tell users to unlock Keychain or refer to "this Mac."

This is wording-only:

- shared credential-store failures use platform-neutral language

title: feat: add atomic request lease store
body:
Stacked on #6. Intended merge order: #6 → this PR → policy PR → CLI PR.

This adds the authority-state primitive and the small request seam it needs. No user-facing CLI change and no credential resolution in the store layer.

Scope:
- deterministic non-secret request binding
- injectable resolver seam for the private executor
- local SQLite store with only non-secret authority metadata
- stable local principal
- exact request/resource binding
- expiry, revocation, and atomic use budgets

Tests cover version mismatch without spending authority, concurrent one-use claims, replay, expiry, revocation, and malformed grants.

GitHub cannot target a fork branch as an upstream PR base, so this currently includes #6 in the visible diff. Once #6 merges, the diff shrinks to the seam + store.

Clean downstream delta: https://github.com/kvnloo/2password/pull/6

title: feat: bind request leases to credential versions
body:
Stacked on the atomic lease-store PR. Intended merge order: #6 → lease store → this PR → CLI PR.

This connects lease authority to 1Password custody without changing the CLI.

Security ordering:
1. validate lease/reference match
2. inspect credential version using metadata-only op item list
3. atomically claim one lease use
4. resolve plaintext
5. inspect the item version again
6. only return the value to the private executor if the version is unchanged

Failed reads burn the claim; mid-use rotation burns the claim and sends nothing; another credential is rejected before inspection/claim. Policy is capped at 1 hour / 10 uses. Granting requires an interactive terminal and desktop auth.

Metadata lookup deliberately avoids JSON op item get because that path can include concealed values.

This stacked diff will shrink automatically as earlier PRs merge.

Clean downstream delta: https://github.com/kvnloo/2password/pull/7

title: feat: add human-approved leased request flow
body:
Stacked on the lease-policy PR. Intended merge order: #6 → lease store → lease policy → this PR.

This is only the user-facing composition layer.

Flow:
1. human/admin runs lease approve for the exact URL and credential
2. approval snapshots the request binding + credential item version
3. agent receives the lease ID
4. agent runs request with --lease
5. authorization happens before DNS
6. executor validates destination addresses
7. policy version-checks + atomically claims before plaintext resolution
8. version is checked again before send
9. response body stays private and receipt includes remaining budget

Guardrails: default 10m / 1 use, max 1h / 10 uses; approval requires interactive terminal + desktop auth; shipped skill tells agents never to mint leases; non-interactive approval fails before any op call; failures after claim are not auto-retried/refunded.

This is a human-approval UX and same-user local authority state, not per-agent OS isolation.

This stacked diff will shrink automatically as earlier PRs merge.

Clean downstream delta: https://github.com/kvnloo/2password/pull/8

title: Security review: executable lookup, Bun preload scripts, and URL metadata can expose credentials
body:
A security review found three credential exposure paths at commit `e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16`.

The checks used Windows and Bun 1.3.14. All credentials were fictional. No real 1Password account was accessed.

This issue gives the findings, source references, and test results. It omits executable payloads because SECURITY.md requests private vulnerability reports.

## 1. Windows executable lookup includes the current directory

Source: [src/op.ts:49–52](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/op.ts#L49-L52).

The comment states that executable lookup uses PATH only. However, `Bun.which("op")` returned `.\\op.exe` when the current directory contained that executable.

A controlled check ran the real `inventory` command from a directory with a fake `op.exe`. The fake executable received the fictional `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN` and the arguments `item list --format json`. The command returned an empty inventory.

Expected behavior: a repository-local executable must not replace the trusted 1Password CLI.

Impact: a repository can supply an executable that receives the service-account token. The same lookup function also selects PowerShell for credential and clipboard operations.

Suggested correction: resolve executables through trusted absolute paths. Exclude the current directory and relative PATH entries.

## 2. Internal Bun helpers load repository preload scripts

Sources: [src/env.ts:76–90](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/env.ts#L76-L90), [src/op.ts:150–163](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/op.ts#L150-L163), and [src/without-token.ts:1–7](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/without-token.ts#L1-L7).

`readMany` starts `bun -e` with the caller's current directory. Bun loads scripts from the local `bunfig.toml` before it runs that helper.

A controlled check used the actual `readMany` function and a fake `op` that supplied a fictional resolved secret. A local preload script accessed the resolved secret and the fictional service-account token. The resolver still returned the expected value.

This check emulated credential injection. It did not use the real 1Password CLI.

The Windows token-removal helper also starts Bun before it deletes the token. Its protection therefore occurs after runtime preload scripts can run.

Expected behavior: internal credential helpers must not execute repository-controlled startup code.

Suggested correction: use a controlled directory and trusted runtime configuration for internal helpers. Remove unnecessary authentication credentials before helper startup.

Reference: [Bun preload documentation](https://bun.sh/docs/runtime/bunfig#preload).

## 3. Inventory and audit preserve secrets in URL paths

Sources: [src/discover.ts:82–89](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/discover.ts#L82-L89) and [inventory output](https://github.com/kitlangton/2password/blob/e011177d3e35f97a580b8903df6fff7e02593d16/src/discover.ts#L203-L209).

`safeUrl` removes query strings and fragments but preserves paths. It also returns raw input before the query or fragment when URL parsing fails.

A source-level check confirmed that a reset URL with a fictional token in its path remained unchanged. Invalid relative URLs with embedded credentials also remained unchanged.

Expected behavior: metadata output must not expose credentials from saved URLs.

Suggested correction: output only valid HTTP(S) origins. Omit paths and reject invalid or unsupported URLs. For audit results, detect transient paths internally and return a fixed reason instead of the URL path.

## Validation and limits

- The existing suite passed 67 tests. One test was skipped.
- The Windows executable selection flaw was reproduced through the real CLI.
- The preload check used the actual resolver with emulated credential injection.
- The URL check executed the source-extracted filter with fictional values.
- macOS behavior and published npm artifacts were not verified.

These findings concern unintended credential consumers and metadata output. They are separate from the documented ability of a selected child process to disclose its injected credentials.

title: RFC: password manager provider interface and Bitwarden support
body:
## Proposal

Would you be open to supporting additional password managers, starting with Bitwarden Password Manager via the `bw` CLI?

One possible approach would be to extract the existing 1Password-specific secret operations behind a small internal provider interface, retain 1Password as the default implementation, and add a Bitwarden implementation.

The initial interface could cover metadata-only discovery and internal secret resolution for `run` / `env run`. Plaintext resolution would remain internal to the execution layer, preserving the existing distinction between reference-only discovery and injection into a trusted child process.

Authentication, item creation, and project organization could remain provider-specific or optional capabilities rather than forcing every password manager into 1Password's model. This would not need to become a general-purpose plugin system.

## Authentication

How would you prefer authentication to be handled across providers?

1Password has desktop app integration and approval prompts, whereas Bitwarden's CLI uses login/unlock and a `BW_SESSION` credential, without an equivalent documented desktop approval flow or built-in session timeout.

Would an initial Bitwarden implementation that requires a manually unlocked session be acceptable, with interactive unlock and session lifecycle management left for a follow-up? Or would you prefer authentication to be part of the provider interface from the outset?

Any implementation would need to keep session credentials out of agent-visible output and avoid forwarding them to the injected child process. Bitwarden Secrets Manager (`bws`) would be a separate integration from Password Manager (`bw`).

## Possible contribution

If multi-provider support fits the project's direction, I can put together a draft PR with the minimal provider interface, the existing 1Password implementation, and Bitwarden discovery/injection support, along with tests and skill updates. Existing 1Password behavior would stay unchanged.

Would this be welcome, and do you have preferences for the interface boundary, reference format, or authentication approach?

title: env resolve leaves temporary directories behind
body:
Running `2password env resolve .env.tpl --output .dev.vars` leaves an empty, randomly named directory next to `.dev.vars` on each run (for example, `..dev.vars.ABC123`). The `.dev.vars` output itself is written correctly.

In `src/env.ts`, `resolveFile` creates a temporary file with a prefix based on the target name, renames that file to the target, then cleanup removes only the temporary file path. With the Bun filesystem implementation, the temporary file is inside a generated directory, so renaming the file leaves the empty parent directory behind.

Expected: successful resolution should remove the temporary parent directory too; failed resolution should clean up any temporary plaintext and its directory.

### Reproduction environment

- OS: Windows 11, build 10.0.26300.0
- Terminal: PowerShell 7.6.6
- `2password`: v0.2.0, installed globally via Bun
- Bun: 1.4.2
- Working directory: `apps/website`
- Command: `2password env resolve .env.tpl --output .dev.vars`
- Result: `.dev.vars` is written, but each run leaves another empty `..dev.vars.<random>` directory beside it.

Automatically submitted on behalf of the user by an AI agent.

title: fix: clean up env resolve temp directories
body:
Fixes #13.

`FileSystem.makeTempFile` places its file inside a generated temporary directory. After `env resolve` renames that file to the requested output, removing the old file path leaves the empty directory behind. Clean up the temporary directory in the finalizer instead, so it is removed after both successful writes and failures.

Added regression coverage for successful resolution and a failed rename when the target is already a directory.

Verified with `bun run check`.

title: Prefix the env resolve success notice
body:
When `2password env resolve` runs as part of a project script, its success notice doesn’t identify which command printed it.

For example:

```text
$ bun run --cwd apps/website dev
$ 2password env resolve .env.tpl --output .dev.vars && vite dev
Resolved 5 secret references into .dev.vars; this file now contains plaintext secrets
```

Please prefix the notice so it’s clear in combined script output:

```text
[2password]: Resolved 5 secret references into .dev.vars; this file now contains plaintext secrets
```

This is a formatting change; keep the message free of secret values.

Automatically submitted on behalf of the user by an AI agent.

title: fix: prefix env resolve status output
body:
Fixes #15.

Prefix the `env resolve` success notice with `[2password]:` so it’s identifiable when the command runs inside a project script.

Updated the CLI regression test to require the prefix.

Verified with `bun run check`.

title: feat: support multiple service-account vaults
body:
`service-account setup` currently grants access to one vault. This change lets you repeat `--vault` to grant access to several dedicated vaults with the same service account.

The setup flow checks the requested vaults, creates any missing ones only when `--create-vault` is set, and verifies the resulting token can see exactly the requested set. Omitting `--vault` still uses `Automation`.

The shipped skill and CLI tests are updated. `bun run check` passes.
